title: The Neighbor
author: Alexandre Dias
contentWarnings: Themes of being unseen and unremembered
excerpt: The first time she asked him he said always. He had lived in the building, he said, since it was built. She thought he meant since the seventies. She was wrong. In the municipal archive was a photograph from 1928. The building's inauguration. Three figures on the paved path in front of the door. One of them was her neighbor. He had not changed.

chapters.title: Always
chapters.body:
The first time she asked him he said *always.*

She had, on a Tuesday evening in April, come home late from work. She was Ingrid Ostergaard, thirty-nine, a copy editor for a small independent publishing house in Copenhagen, and she had moved into the small apartment on the second floor of the building at Willemoesgade eleven eight months earlier, after the end of a marriage that had, in the last two years of its slow ending, taken a great deal from her. The apartment had been the first place she had lived alone since she was twenty-three. She had chosen it for the quiet street, and for the specific soft light that came in through the tall windows of the sitting room in the afternoons, and for the small rent she could afford on her own salary. She had, in the eight months, come to like it. She had also come to know the small careful particularities of the building — the tenant on the ground floor who played piano in the mornings on Saturdays, the tenant across the hall who received a great many small brown packages, the specific old smell of the stairwell that she thought was linoleum and the specific new smell she thought was the paint on the freshly repainted railings.

She had not, in the eight months, known her neighbor.

Her neighbor lived in the apartment across the small landing from her own. His name, according to the small brass plate beside his door, was H. Aagaard. She had seen him perhaps six or seven times in the eight months — coming home in the evening as he was going out, or crossing him on the stairs — and had, on each occasion, nodded politely and said the small ordinary Danish greeting one said to a neighbor one did not know. He had, on each occasion, nodded and said the same. He had, she thought, been perhaps seventy. He was a small neat man with white hair combed back from his forehead and small round glasses and a specific kind of grey wool coat that she thought was expensive but had been kept, over what looked like many years, in the specific careful way that made the age of a good coat difficult to guess.

She had not, in the eight months, exchanged with him any words beyond *goddag* and *godaften.*

On that particular Tuesday evening in April, she had come home to find him standing on the small landing between their two apartments. He had been standing at his own door. He had been, from what she could tell in the small light of the stairwell, going through his pockets. He had, she gathered as she came up the last flight of stairs, been looking for his key.

She had said, in the small friendly way one said such things to a neighbor: *lost your key?*

He had looked up. He had smiled, in the small polite way of an older Danish man who was pleased to be spoken to but not to be delayed. He had said: *no. Just — pockets are a mystery, sometimes.*

She had said: *they are.*

He had, at that moment, found his key. He had held it up in a small triumphant gesture. He had said: *there.*

She had, unlocking her own door, glanced over at him.

She had said, without really thinking about it: *how long have you lived in the building?*

He had said, in his small polite voice: *always.*

She had turned her head.

She had said: *always?*

He had looked at her. His small round glasses had reflected the light of the stairwell in a way that had, for a moment, made his eyes hard to see. He had said: *since it was built. Yes.*

He had nodded to her, and had opened his door, and had gone inside.

She had stood on the landing for a moment, with her key in her own door.

She had thought: *he means his family owned it.*

She had thought: *he means since the seventies. He is old. To a man of seventy, that is always.*

She had gone into her apartment.

She had, over the course of the following evening, mostly forgotten about the conversation. She had, however, that Friday, when she had run into the ground-floor tenant — the piano-playing woman, whose name she had learned in the second month was Vibeke and who was in her sixties and had, throughout Ingrid's time in the building, been friendly in the small unpressured Danish way — asked her, in passing:

*How old is the building?*

Vibeke had said: *the building? It went up in the twenties. I think 1926. Something like that.*

Ingrid had said: *and how long has Mr. Aagaard lived here?*

Vibeke had said: *Mr. Aagaard?*

Ingrid had said: *the man across the hall from me. On the second floor.*

Vibeke had said, with a small pleasant frown of consideration: *oh. Mr. Aagaard. I have wondered about that, actually. He was here when I moved in. That was twenty-two years ago.*

Ingrid had said: *and he had been here a long time then?*

Vibeke had said: *I never asked. But — yes, I think so. He seems, doesn't he, to have always been here.*

Vibeke had laughed, in the small self-conscious way of someone who had said something slightly odd. She had said: *sorry. I do not know why I put it like that.*

Ingrid had said: *no, no. That is what he said.*

Vibeke had looked at her.

Vibeke had said: *pardon?*

Ingrid had said: *I asked him, on Tuesday, how long he had lived here. He said always.*

Vibeke had, for a moment, been quiet.

She had said, then, with a small careful shrug: *well. He is old.*

Ingrid had said: *he is.*

They had, after that, changed the subject.

—

Ingrid had, over the following weeks, begun to notice him more.

She had begun to notice him without deciding to. She had come home on the following Wednesday and he had been standing on the small landing, again, at his own door, looking through his pockets. She had come home on the Monday after and he had been at the door again. She had, on a Saturday morning, been going down to the shop and had passed him on the stairs going up. She had, on the same Saturday afternoon, been coming back from the shop and had passed him again going down.

She had, on each occasion, said the small ordinary greeting. He had, on each occasion, said the same. He had, on none of the occasions, seemed to recognize her.

This had been, at first, only a small oddness. Older men were sometimes forgetful. Older men who lived alone and did not much interact with their neighbors were, in her experience, particularly forgetful of faces. She had not, in her first apartment in Copenhagen at twenty-three, been remembered by the elderly woman across the hall from her for the whole of the two years she had lived there, and this had not, at the time, seemed strange.

But she had begun to notice, over the following weeks, that Mr. Aagaard's forgetfulness had a particular quality. He did not fail to recognize her in the small vague way of an old man who did not remember faces. He looked at her, on each meeting, with the specific *polite* attention of a man who had, for the first time, encountered a stranger in his stairwell — a small careful courtesy, a small pleasant greeting, and then a small pleasant continuation of his own business. He did not, ever, in any small way, indicate that he had seen her before.

She had, on the seventh or eighth of these meetings, done a small experiment.

She had, coming up the stairs one Wednesday evening, said, when she had reached the landing: *good evening, Mr. Aagaard.*

She had used his name.

He had turned, from where he had been going through his pockets at his door, and had looked at her with the same specific polite attention. He had, after a small pause, said: *good evening. I do not think we have —*

He had stopped.

He had said: *I am sorry. My name?*

She had said: *Aagaard. Isn't it? The small plate by your door.*

He had said, in a small pleased way: *ah. Yes. Aagaard. Yes, that is my name.*

She had said: *I am Ingrid. I live across the hall.*

He had said: *I did not know I had a neighbor.*

She had said: *for eight months. Since August.*

He had said: *ah.*

He had said, then, in his small polite way: *well. It is very nice to meet you, Ingrid.*

He had, at that moment, found his key. He had turned to his door and had let himself in.

Ingrid had stood on the landing.

She had thought, quietly: *he has forgotten every single time.*

She had thought: *he has forgotten every single time I have said goddag to him. He has forgotten that I live across the hall. He has forgotten my face. He is not, in the ordinary way of an old man, becoming forgetful. He is, in some more definite way, not able to hold me.*

She had gone into her apartment.

She had sat on the sofa for a long time.

She had thought about how many other people, in the small closed world of the building, had also been, over the years, not held by Mr. Aagaard.

She had thought about Vibeke, and about the small hesitant way Vibeke had said *he seems to have always been here.*

She had thought, in a small unformed way that had frightened her slightly, that it was possible that Vibeke had also been, throughout her twenty-two years, not held.

—

She had, on the following Saturday, done something she had not intended.

She had waited, on the landing, for him to come out.

She had done this without really admitting to herself that she was doing it. She had gone down to the shop in the morning, and had, on coming back, sat on the small step at the top of the stairs — which was in the small alcove just beyond the landing, and was not visible from her own door or from his — and had made herself busy with her phone, and had, in this small pretense of ordinary occupation, waited.

He had come out at eleven-fifteen.

He had opened his door and had come out onto the landing in his grey wool coat and his small round glasses, and had, in the specific small careful way she had, over the last weeks, come to expect, locked his door behind him. He had turned to go down the stairs.

He had seen her, sitting on the small step.

He had, for a moment, stopped.

She had looked up from her phone.

She had said, in the small pleasant way one said such things: *good morning, Mr. Aagaard.*

He had, for a long moment, looked at her.

His face had, for that long moment, been quite still. It had not had, in that moment, the small polite courtesy she had come to expect. It had had a different expression — the specific small careful look of a man who was looking at something he had not, until that moment, been sure was there.

He had said, at last: *good morning.*

He had not said her name.

He had, after a moment, added: *do we — do we know each other?*

She had said: *I live across the hall. From you. Ingrid. I have said good morning to you nine or ten times.*

He had said: *ah.*

He had, for another moment, looked at her.

He had said, more quietly: *how long have you lived across the hall from me.*

She had said: *since August.*

He had said, still more quietly: *this August.*

She had said: *yes.*

He had said, and his voice had, at this sentence, changed in some small definite way that she had not been able, afterwards, quite to describe: *and you have said good morning to me nine or ten times.*

She had said: *yes.*

He had said: *and I have not, on any of those occasions, remembered you.*

She had said: *no.*

He had, for a long moment, been quiet.

He had said, at last: *I am sorry.*

He had said: *it is very good to meet you, Ingrid.*

He had turned. He had walked down the stairs.

She had sat on the small step for a very long time after he had gone.

She had understood, sitting there, that his voice at the end had not been the voice of an old man discovering he was becoming forgetful. It had been the voice of a man who had, at that moment, understood something he had long suspected — the specific small tired voice of a man who had been told something he had, in his own way, already known.

She had understood, further, that whatever he had known, he had known for a long time.

She had understood, finally, that whatever was happening in the building — the small careful forgetting, the way Vibeke had lived twenty-two years without ever quite being remembered, the small pleasant *always* he had said on the first evening — was something Mr. Aagaard had, in his own small polite way, been *managing.*

She had gotten up. She had gone into her apartment.

She had, for the first time in eight months, locked her door from the inside during the day.

chapters.title: The Photographs
chapters.body:
She began, over the following weeks, to look.

She did this carefully. She did it in the small quiet way of a woman who had, throughout her adult life, done research on unremarkable things for the small publishing house she worked for, and who had learned, over that time, how to find out what a small ordinary sort of person could find out about another person in the ordinary records of a small orderly country.

She began at the small municipal archive.

She had, on a Wednesday afternoon in May, taken a half-day of leave from work and had gone to the archive in the specific small hope that the building at Willemoesgade eleven had, at some point in its history, been the subject of some documentation that included the names of its tenants. She had not been sure what she would find. Danish archives were, as a rule, thorough, but they were also — for reasons of privacy — not always accessible in the way an amateur researcher might want.

She had found, in the archive, several things.

She had found the original building permits from 1926. She had found the name of the architect, and of the small firm that had built the building, and of the family that had commissioned it — a small merchant family named Kjærgaard who had, at the time, owned three buildings in the neighborhood and had commissioned the fourth. She had found, in the ordinary way of Danish records, the list of the first tenants who had moved in during 1927.

She had scanned the list.

She had, halfway down, seen the name *H. Aagaard.*

She had, for a moment, thought this must be a coincidence. Aagaard was a common Danish name. She had, in the last two decades, known perhaps five or six Aagaards. It was, statistically, entirely reasonable that a building at which she now lived across the hall from an old man named H. Aagaard should, ninety-nine years ago, have had a first tenant named the same.

She had, all the same, made a note of the name.

She had, later that afternoon, gone to the small photographic archive that was housed in the same building. Copenhagen kept, in its municipal collections, a great many photographs of ordinary buildings and ordinary streets, taken over the last century for various small reasons of urban documentation. She had, over the last few years of her work at the publishing house, become moderately familiar with the collection. She had known that it included, if one searched by address, whatever photographs had been taken of any given building at any point in its history.

She had searched by *Willemoesgade 11.*

The collection had produced, without any particular difficulty, seven photographs.

The earliest had been from 1928, taken by a photographer named Andersen who had, in that year, documented a range of the new residential buildings that had gone up in that section of the city. It had shown the building from the street. It had shown the small paved path leading up to the front door, and the small entrance, and the tall narrow windows of the ground floor. It had shown, standing on the small paved path in front of the door, three figures — the architect, according to the small handwritten note on the back of the print, and two of the tenants who had wished to be photographed with him on the occasion of the building's inauguration.

One of the tenants had been an unremarkable middle-aged woman in a hat.

The other had been a small neat man in a grey wool coat and small round glasses.

Ingrid had looked at the photograph for a long time.

She had, at last, gotten up from the small reading desk. She had walked to the counter, and had asked, in the small polite way one asked such things of an archivist, whether she might make a reproduction of the photograph for her personal records.

She had gone home.

—

She had, in her sitting room that evening, put the reproduction on the small coffee table.

She had turned on the small lamp beside the sofa. She had sat on the sofa with the reproduction on the coffee table in front of her. She had looked at it.

The small neat man in the photograph had been, unmistakably, the same man who lived across the hall from her.

He had not been an ancestor. He had not been a resemblance. It had been the same face, the same small round glasses, the same specific carriage of the shoulders, the same grey wool coat. The photograph had been taken in 1928. The man in it had been perhaps sixty. If he had been sixty in 1928, he would now, in April of the year Ingrid was looking at the photograph, be one hundred and fifty-seven years old.

He had, when she had seen him on the landing that morning, been perhaps seventy.

Ingrid had sat with the photograph for a long time.

She had, at last, telephoned Vibeke.

She had said, when Vibeke had answered: *Vibeke. It is Ingrid. I know it is late. May I come down for a moment?*

Vibeke had said: *of course. Come down.*

Ingrid had put the reproduction into a small folder. She had put on her cardigan. She had gone down two flights of stairs to Vibeke's apartment.

Vibeke had opened the door in a small robe over her pyjamas. She had made tea. They had sat, at the small kitchen table, and Ingrid had, without ceremony, put the reproduction on the table between them.

Vibeke had looked at it for a moment.

Vibeke had said: *this is 1928.*

Ingrid had said: *yes.*

Vibeke had said, quietly: *and this man.*

She had pointed to the small neat man in the grey wool coat.

Ingrid had said: *yes.*

Vibeke had, for a long moment, been quiet.

She had said, at last: *I have wondered.*

Ingrid had said: *have you.*

Vibeke had said: *for many years. I did not — I have not — I have not known how to think about it. I have known him for twenty-two years. He has not changed. He has been, in every year, exactly the same. His coat has not changed. His glasses have not changed. His hair has not changed. He has, for twenty-two years, been the same seventy-year-old man.*

Ingrid had said: *and before you?*

Vibeke had said: *my mother lived in this apartment before me. She lived here for thirty-one years. She died in it. She had, when I was a small girl visiting, sometimes said to me — she had said, once — that she had wondered whether Mr. Aagaard was ever going to move out.*

Ingrid had said: *she said his name.*

Vibeke had said: *she said his name.*

They had sat with the tea.

Vibeke had said: *my mother was born in 1938. She moved in as a young woman in 1962. And she said, in 1985 or so — she said to me, when I was seventeen — that Mr. Aagaard had been across the hall for the entire time she had lived here, and had, in her opinion, not aged a day.*

Ingrid had said: *and you have said nothing.*

Vibeke had said: *to whom?*

Ingrid had, for a moment, been unable to answer.

Vibeke had said: *I have said nothing because there is nothing to say. He does not — he does not do anything. He does not bother anyone. He does not — he is not — he is a small polite old man in a grey coat, and he lives across the hall from you, and he has, in his own way, done no one any harm in one hundred years of doing it. What would I say?*

Ingrid had said: *but he does not remember anyone.*

Vibeke had said: *no.*

Ingrid had said: *he does not, for you, either.*

Vibeke had said: *no.*

Ingrid had said: *he does not, then, know that you have lived here for twenty-two years.*

Vibeke had said: *he does not, from what I can tell, know that anyone has lived here.*

Ingrid had sat with this.

She had said: *and yet he opens his door every evening, and locks his door every morning, and goes out and comes back, and does what he has always done, and has done since 1927.*

Vibeke had said: *yes.*

Ingrid had said: *what does he do, do you think.*

Vibeke had said: *I do not know.*

Vibeke had said: *I have thought about it. I have thought — because I am old, and one thinks about these things — I have thought that whatever he does, he does not do it for us. He does not do it for the tenants. He does it for — for the building. For the walls. He does it because the building requires that he do it. He locks his door. He unlocks his door. He goes out. He comes back. He does this because this is what a tenant in the building does. And he is, in some way I cannot explain, a tenant that the building has kept.*

Ingrid had said: *for one hundred years.*

Vibeke had said: *for one hundred years. Perhaps longer.*

Ingrid had said: *and the rest of us.*

Vibeke had said: *what about us.*

Ingrid had said: *are we tenants? Or are we — are we something else.*

Vibeke had, for a very long moment, looked at her.

Vibeke had said, at last: *I do not know.*

Vibeke had said: *I have thought about that too. I have thought — I have thought, sometimes, that the reason we are not remembered by him is not because he has a fault. It is because we are not, from his perspective — from the building's perspective — we are not the residents. We are the visitors. He is the resident. He has always been the resident. We come and we go, sometimes for a night, sometimes for thirty years, sometimes for a hundred, but we are — we are, in the arithmetic of the building — passing through. And he is not.*

Ingrid had said: *and the building loves him.*

Vibeke had said: *I do not think of it as love. I think of it as — as a kind of care. The building takes care of him. The building keeps him. The building forgets us because we are not, from its perspective, worth remembering.*

Ingrid had said, quietly: *I do not want to be a person who is not worth remembering.*

Vibeke had said: *I know.*

They had sat with the tea.

Vibeke had said, at last: *what will you do.*

Ingrid had said: *I do not know.*

Vibeke had said: *I have thought about moving, from time to time. I have not, in twenty-two years, done it. I do not — I do not want, at this point, to move. I am old. I have made my peace with what the building is.*

She had said: *but you are still young. You have the years I do not have. You could go somewhere the building was — was ordinary. Where you would be, to whoever lived across the hall from you, remembered.*

Ingrid had, for a moment, considered this.

She had said, quietly: *would he notice, if I left.*

Vibeke had said: *no.*

Ingrid had said: *would the building notice.*

Vibeke had said: *I do not know.*

Ingrid had said: *and the person who came after me.*

Vibeke had said: *she would be like you. And like me. And she would meet him on the landing, and he would say goddag, and she would say goddag, and she would live her small life across the hall from him for a year or a decade or forty years, and he would never once know she was there.*

Ingrid had said: *and he would go on.*

Vibeke had said: *he would go on.*

Ingrid had, at that moment, understood something she had not, until that moment, quite been willing to name.

She had understood that Mr. Aagaard was not, in any sense that mattered, alive. He was a shape the building maintained. He was the one thing the building bothered to keep. Everything else about the building — the piano on Saturday mornings, the small brown packages, the tenants who came and went — was, in the small arithmetic Vibeke had described, of no consequence. Only Mr. Aagaard mattered. The building kept him because he was, in some way she could not name, what the building was *for.*

She had, further, understood something else.

She had understood that the small polite courtesy Mr. Aagaard had shown her on the Saturday morning, when he had, for a long moment, looked at her with the specific quiet attention of a man who was looking at something he had not been sure was there — had been a moment of recognition.

He had, for that moment, seen her.

He had not, on any subsequent meeting, seen her again.

She had, all the same, been seen once.

She had wondered, walking back up the stairs to her apartment that night with the folder under her arm, whether that once had been enough — whether it had, in the small quiet arithmetic of the building, been enough to make her, in some way, present.

chapters.title: Tenant
chapters.body:
She did not, in the end, move.

She thought about it. She thought about it every day for the following two weeks. She spoke to the landlord, quietly, about the possibility of finding another apartment. She looked at three. She went, on a Saturday afternoon, to see a small apartment in a different neighborhood that had, when she had walked through it, seemed to her perfectly nice.

She had, that evening, come back to Willemoesgade eleven, and had sat in her own sitting room in the specific soft light of six o'clock, and had understood that she was not going to leave.

She had understood this without deliberation. She had spent forty-seven years of her life, or she thought she had — she was thirty-nine at that particular Saturday evening, but forty-seven was the age at which she had, over the course of the last two years, been living somewhere in the back of her mind — trying to be a woman a certain kind of husband would find memorable. She had, in the end, failed. He had not remembered her — not in any way that had mattered. He had gone.

She had come here.

She had come here to a small apartment across the hall from a man who was less able to remember her than any human being she had ever met. She had come here to a building that considered her, in Vibeke's phrase, a person passing through. She had come here to a specific quiet consignment to being ordinary, unremarkable, unheld.

She had thought, sitting in the sofa in the soft light: *I have made my peace with not being remembered.*

She had thought: *I have made my peace with it because I have already been not remembered. I have already been the wife whose husband did not remember why he had married her. I have already been the child whose parents did not remember to ask her, before they died, what she had wanted. I have been not-remembered for the whole of my life. I do not need Mr. Aagaard to remember me. I do not need the building to remember me. I am not, and have never been, a person whom things remember.*

She had thought, and this thought had come with a small strange comfort: *the building is honest about it. My husband was not.*

She had made a small decision.

She had, from that Saturday evening onward, ceased to try to be remembered by Mr. Aagaard.

She had, on the following Monday morning, encountered him on the stairs, and had, when he had said his small polite good morning, said her small polite good morning back, and had not offered her name. She had, on the Tuesday evening, come home to find him at his door, and had, when she had passed him, nodded and said godaften, and had gone into her own apartment.

She had, over the following weeks, seen him perhaps ten or twelve times. She had, on each occasion, said the ordinary greeting. She had, on none of the occasions, tried to make him hold her. She had, in some small definite way, given up on him.

She had, in giving up on him, been surprised to find that this was, in fact, easier than she had expected.

She had come, over those weeks, to a small quiet arrangement with the building. She was here. She would be here for as long as she was here. She would not be remembered. She would, when she left — whether in a year or in thirty — be forgotten, more or less immediately, by everything about the building except perhaps Vibeke, who might, if Vibeke outlived her tenure, mention her once to some future tenant who moved in. That would be all right. That would be more than she had, in her marriage, expected.

She had, in the third week of this arrangement, come home to find something on her doormat.

—

It had been a small brown envelope.

It had not had a stamp. It had not had a return address. It had had, in a small careful hand, her name on the front. Ingrid Ostergaard. Nothing else.

She had picked it up. She had gone into her apartment. She had, at the small table in her kitchen, opened the envelope.

Inside the envelope had been a single small photograph.

The photograph had been taken, from the small distance and small angle of it, from the landing at the top of the second-floor stairs. It had shown her own apartment door. It had shown, standing at her own door, herself — from the back, in her cardigan, in the specific pose of a woman unlocking her door with a bag of groceries in her other hand.

The photograph had been recent. She had recognized her cardigan and her jeans and the specific weight of the small canvas bag of groceries. She had been, when the photograph had been taken, coming home from the shop the previous Tuesday.

On the back of the photograph, in the same small careful hand as the envelope, had been written:

*My dear neighbor,*

*I did want to tell you: I have, in my way, kept you.*

*— H. A.*

Ingrid had sat at the small kitchen table for a long time.

She had understood, sitting there, several things.

She had understood, first, that Mr. Aagaard had taken the photograph. He had, at some moment the previous Tuesday when she had been coming home, been on the landing above, and had, with some small camera she had not noticed, taken her picture. He had, in the days since, developed the print. He had written on the back. He had, at some hour of the last day, put it in the envelope and had put the envelope on her doormat.

She had understood, second, that this had cost him some considerable effort. Mr. Aagaard did not, so far as she had been able to determine, use his memory for anything ordinary. He did not, as she now knew, remember his neighbors. He did not, presumably, easily hold in his mind the small work of taking a photograph, printing it, writing on it, and delivering it — the small chain of intentions required for such an act.

He had, all the same, done it.

She had understood, third, that the phrase *I have kept you* was not what she had first thought it was. She had, on the first reading, thought it was a small formal Danish courtesy — *jeg har holdt Dem*, roughly meaning *I have thought of you* or *I have kept you in mind.* But she had, on the second reading, understood that it was, in fact, more literal than that. He had kept her. He had, by the small definite act of taking the photograph and holding it and writing on it, made a small definite record of her presence in his life. He had, in some small way that had cost him what she guessed was a considerable portion of his available attention, refused to forget her.

She had understood, fourth, that this was a gift.

It was a gift he had made only once — she had understood this, quietly, as she looked at the photograph — because it was, for him, all that could be made. He could not, in any general way, remember her. He could not, going forward, greet her by name on the stairs. He could not join the small community of people who noticed one another. He could, however, at some considerable cost, make one small record.

He had made it.

He had made it for her.

She had, at the small kitchen table, sat with the photograph for a long time. She had, at last, taken it into the sitting room. She had, from the bookshelf, taken down a small book — a slim volume of poems by a Danish poet whom she had, at seventeen, loved — and had opened it to a specific page. She had put the small photograph between the pages. She had returned the book to the shelf.

She had gone to bed.

—

She had lived at Willemoesgade eleven for the following seventeen years.

She had, over those years, seen Mr. Aagaard many times. She had, on each occasion, said her small polite greeting. He had, on each occasion, said the same. He had, on none of the occasions, indicated that he remembered her.

She had, on none of the occasions, minded.

She had known, when she saw him — she had known always — that he had, in his own way, once kept her. She had known that the photograph was on the shelf. She had known that the small book contained, in its middle pages, a record of a specific afternoon on which she had, in some small way that mattered, been present in the building. She had not, in the seventeen years, ever taken the photograph out to look at it again. She had not needed to. She had known where it was.

She had, in the fifth year of the seventeen, become friends with Vibeke, in the specific slow way of Danish friendship. They had, over the following twelve years, drunk a great deal of tea together. They had, on many evenings, spoken about the building. They had, on none of those evenings, spoken about Mr. Aagaard.

Vibeke had died in the fifteenth year of the seventeen, quietly, in her own apartment, at the age of eighty-one. Ingrid had, at the funeral, been one of the small number of people who had come. She had, in Vibeke's belongings, been given by Vibeke's daughter a small object Vibeke had, in her will, specifically requested be given to Ingrid.

The object had been a small brown envelope.

Inside the envelope had been a single small photograph.

It had shown Vibeke, from the back, standing at the piano in her sitting room, playing. It had been taken, from the small angle of it, from the doorway of her apartment.

On the back, in the same small careful hand, had been written:

*My dear neighbor,*

*I did want to tell you: I have, in my way, kept you.*

*— H. A.*

Ingrid had, when she had seen it, sat down on Vibeke's sofa in the empty apartment, and had cried quietly for perhaps a full ten minutes.

She had, then, put the small photograph into the pocket of her cardigan, and had walked upstairs to her own apartment, and had put it into the same book of poems where her own photograph had been for twenty-two years.

She had understood, that afternoon, that Mr. Aagaard had been keeping Vibeke too.

She had understood, further, that he had, in his careful small way, kept every one of them. Every tenant who had ever lived in the building for the ninety-nine years he had been across the hall. He had, at some point in each of their lives, taken one photograph. He had written on the back. He had delivered the envelope. He had, in some way she could not entirely understand, refused to permit the building's ordinary forgetting to be complete.

He had, in this way, held them all.

She had, in her own way, been in a small quiet community she had not known she was in.

—

She had left Willemoesgade eleven in the seventeenth year.

She had left because she had, at fifty-six, been offered a position with a larger publishing house in a smaller town, and had, after some months of thinking about it, taken the position, and had moved to a small house of her own in that town. She had, on the day of her departure, gone across the landing and had knocked on Mr. Aagaard's door.

He had opened it.

He had said: *good morning.*

She had said: *I am moving out today. I am moving out of Copenhagen. I wanted to say goodbye.*

He had, for a moment, looked at her.

He had said: *have we met?*

She had said: *many times.*

He had said: *ah.*

He had said, in the small polite way: *well. Safe travels.*

She had said: *thank you.*

She had said: *and thank you — I did not want to leave without — thank you for the photograph.*

He had, at the word *photograph*, looked at her more carefully.

He had said: *the photograph.*

She had said: *the one you took. Many years ago. The one you left on my doormat.*

He had, for a very long moment, looked at her.

He had said, at last, quietly: *I do not remember taking a photograph.*

She had said: *I know.*

He had said, still more quietly: *but I did take one.*

She had said: *you did.*

He had said: *did I write on the back.*

She had said: *you did.*

He had said: *what did I write.*

She had said: *you wrote — I have, in my way, kept you.*

He had, at those words, done something Ingrid had not, in seventeen years, seen him do. He had smiled. It had not been the small polite courtesy she had come to know. It had been a small warm private smile, of the kind a very old man might make on remembering a small good thing he had done a long time ago that had gone, in the intervening years, entirely unremarked.

He had said: *ah.*

He had said: *yes. That is what I would have written.*

He had said, very quietly: *I am glad you kept it.*

She had said: *I did.*

He had, for a moment, been quiet.

He had said: *goodbye, then.*

She had said: *goodbye, Mr. Aagaard.*

He had, at that name, looked at her.

He had said: *is that my name.*

She had said: *it is on the small plate by your door.*

He had said: *ah. Yes. Aagaard. Yes.*

He had smiled at her, once more, the small polite courtesy she had come to know.

He had gone back inside.

—

She had moved out that afternoon.

She had, in the years since, lived quietly in her small house in the small town. She had, over the years, come to know her neighbors there — a young family on one side, an old couple on the other — and had, in the ordinary way of a small town, been remembered by them. She had, in the ordinary way of her ordinary life, made small friends and had small conversations and had lived a small unremarkable life.

She had, in the small drawer of her bedside table, kept the two photographs. Her own, and Vibeke's. She had, from time to time, on quiet evenings, taken them out and looked at them.

She had, in her seventy-fourth year, died — of a small quiet stroke, in the middle of the night, in the small back bedroom of her small house — and had, in her will, left the two photographs to no one. She had specified only that they were to be, along with certain other small objects of her private life, cremated with her.

They had been.

The building at Willemoesgade eleven had, at the time of Ingrid's death, still been there. Mr. Aagaard had, at the time of her death, still been in his apartment across the hall from what had once been hers. He had, in the intervening years, taken perhaps twelve more photographs of perhaps twelve more tenants. He had made his small careful envelopes. He had left them on doormats.

He is, so far as anyone knows, still there.

He is not, in any way that matters, remembered by the world outside the building. His face does not appear in any modern photograph but the one from 1928, and that photograph is, in the archive, catalogued only as *inauguration of Willemoesgade 11.* His name is on no census. His name is on no register. His name is on the small brass plate beside his door and nowhere else.

But there are, scattered across the world, in the personal belongings of the tenants and the descendants of tenants who have lived across the hall from him for the last hundred years, a small number of small brown envelopes. Each envelope contains one photograph. Each photograph shows an ordinary person, from the back, in an ordinary moment of an ordinary life.

On the back of each is the same small sentence in the same small careful hand.

*I have, in my way, kept you.*

If anyone were to gather them together — and no one has, and probably no one will — they would find that they constitute, in their small quiet accumulation, a hundred years of a small building's actual residents. Not the tenant of record. Not the tenant of paperwork. The person who had, at some specific moment of their life in the building, been present enough to be seen.

Mr. Aagaard has, in his own way, kept them all.

He goes on keeping.

He will, so long as the building stands and there is anyone across the hall to keep, go on keeping.
